memories.memory_text: I was told by Elaine that there was a problem with my story about having a grown son with Jan in 1935, and I realized she was right to question it.

grounded_facts: Paul makes a decision to disclose a previously unrevealed truth after realizing Elaine's confusion about the timeline involving his son with Jan.
memories.memory_text: I realized Elaine was confused about how I could have a grown son back in 1935, and I decided it was time to tell her the truth, so I asked her if she felt up to a walk to keep talking.

grounded_facts: Paul and Elaine arrive at the storage shacks located in the woods, marking the start of a significant revelation.
memories.memory_text: I brought Elaine along the wooded path to the storage shacks, both of us wearing ponchos as we arrived.

grounded_facts: Paul reassures Elaine that the thing he wants to show her is not scary after she expresses concern.
memories.memory_text: I told Elaine that the thing I wanted to show her wasn't scary when she asked me, and I meant it—no, not really.

grounded_facts: Paul offers his hand to Elaine, who accepts it, as a gesture of comfort and connection.
memories.memory_text: I offered my hand to Elaine, and she took it, as a small gesture to comfort her and keep us connected.

grounded_facts: Paul directs Elaine's attention to Mr. Jingles, sharing a meaningful secret.
memories.memory_text: I touched Elaine's arm and said, 'There,' guiding her attention to share the secret of Mr. Jingles.

grounded_facts: Paul brings Elaine to the shack and shows her an old mouse, Mr. Jingles, who is still alive despite his age and frailty.
memories.memory_text: I got down on the floor and called Mr. Jingles over, showing Elaine the old mouse who is still alive despite his frailty and age.

grounded_facts: Paul brings Elaine to a shack to show her Mr. Jingles, leading to emotional revelations and a confrontation with Brad.
memories.memory_text: I brought Elaine to the shack to show her Mr. Jingles, and when she started forward, I held her back, knowing this moment would bring both revelation and confrontation.

grounded_facts: Brad Dolan enters the shack unexpectedly and threatens to kill Mr. Jingles with a garden hoe.
memories.memory_text: I was in the shack with Mr. Jingles when Brad Dolan suddenly burst in, grabbed a rusted garden hoe, shoved me hard against the wall, and threatened to kill my mouse, calling me a senile fucker.

grounded_facts: Elaine uses her political connection to threaten Brad's employment at Georgia Pines.
memories.memory_text: I heard Elaine warn Brad that she could end his days of employment at Georgia Pines by making a phone call, claiming she was the grandmother of the Speaker of the Georgia House.

grounded_facts: Elaine angrily confronts Brad after he shoves Paul and threatens Mr. Jingles.
memories.memory_text: I saw Elaine step in when Brad shoved me and threatened Mr. Jingles, and she shouted at him with such anger, telling him to get out and calling him ignorant.

grounded_facts: Paul tells Elaine that he has lived over a century due to a supernatural gift from John Coffey.
Paul tells Elaine that John Coffey gave him a supernatural gift that made him live for over a century.
memories.memory_text: I told Elaine that I'm over a century old because John Coffey gave me a supernatural gift, and I haven't even had a cold since—I've had to watch everyone I love die, including my wife, my son, and now I'll have to see her go too.

grounded_facts: A funeral service held for Elaine Connelly, with Paul in attendance.
memories.memory_text: I walked up the aisle and saw Elaine lying in the open casket during her funeral service.

grounded_facts: Paul voice-over reveals his belief that surviving while others die is his punishment for executing John Coffey, whom he views as a miracle of God.
memories.memory_text: I told myself that my punishment is living on while others are gone, because I let John Coffey be executed—I killed a miracle of God.

grounded_facts: Paul lays a rose on the casket of Elaine Connelly during her funeral, symbolizing mourning and guilt.
memories.memory_text: I placed a rose on Elaine's casket to honor her and carry my guilt with me.

grounded_facts: A funeral or memorial gathering at the cemetery where Paul is present as the casket is lowered.
memories.memory_text: I stood at the graveside as they lowered the casket, and then I turned and walked away.

grounded_facts: Paul voice-over reveals his deep emotional despair and wish for death, indicating a significant internal state.
memories.memory_text: I admitted to myself that I have no illusions of living forever, and that I will have wished for death long before it comes—I wish for it already.

grounded_facts: Paul calls out to Mr. Jingles upon seeing him and expresses concern, asking where he's been and if he's hungry.
memories.memory_text: I called out to Mr. Jingles when I saw him and asked where he'd been, telling him I'd been worried and asking if he was hungry.

grounded_facts: Paul discovers the missing mouse, Mr. Jingles, returning and appearing worn out from under the restraint room door, then picks him up gently.
memories.memory_text: I saw Mr. Jingles peering out from under the restraint room door, looking worn out, so I bent down and gently picked him up, cupping him in my hands as I turned back up the Green Mile.

grounded_facts: Paul lies awake at night, reflecting on lost loved ones, particularly Jan, and contemplates the inevitability of death, symbolized by the long walk of the Green Mile. He questions how much longer he has to live, prompted by the longevity of Mr. Jingles.
memories.memory_text: I lie awake thinking about all the people I've loved who are now gone, especially my beautiful Jan—I lost her so many years ago. I know we each owe a death, with no exceptions, but sometimes, oh God, the Green Mile feels so long, and I wonder how much longer I have to walk it.

grounded_facts: Billy is dragged to the restraint room and locked in as punishment for humiliating Brutal.
memories.memory_text: I saw Billy being dragged to the restraint room and locked in after I ordered his punishment.

grounded_facts: Billy spews liquefied Moon Pie into Brutal's face as a prank, then mocks him with a racist caricature.
After spewing chocolate on Brutal, Billy laughs and uses a racist stereotype to mock him.
memories.memory_text: I was inspecting the cell when Billy suddenly spat liquefied chocolate in my face, and then he laughed and mocked me with a racist caricature, saying 'Li'l Black Sambo, yassuh, boss, yassuh, howdoo you do?' while I wiped the sludge off.

grounded_facts: Paul tells Del that important visitors want to see Mr. Jingles perform, which delights Del.
Del is informed that important visitors, including a politician, want to see Mr. Jingles perform, leading him to prepare and leave his cell.
A scheduled event where Del will demonstrate Mr. Jingles' tricks for visiting dignitaries, including a state politician.
memories.memory_text: I heard Paul tell me to grab my things because important visitors, including a politician from the state capital, wanted to see Mr. Jingles perform, and I felt proud as I gathered my props and left my cell.

grounded_facts: Coffey tells Del to impress the audience, echoing Harry's words.
memories.memory_text: I remember Coffey telling me to impress the audience, echoing what Harry had said, just before I went to perform.

grounded_facts: Percy smirks and rolls his eyes as Del passes by on the way to the performance.
memories.memory_text: As I passed by on the way to the performance, I saw Percy smirk and roll his eyes at me.

grounded_facts: Toot moves into Del's cell to impersonate him while Del is away.
memories.memory_text: I saw Toot hurry down and take Del's place in the cell.

grounded_facts: Del returns with Mr. Jingles, having successfully entertained other inmates, creating a rare moment of joy and acceptance.
memories.memory_text: I escorted Del back with Mr. Jingles on his shoulder, carrying the cigar box and spool like a magician's assistant, and I heard him say the other inmates loved Mr. Jingles and were laughing and cheering.

grounded_facts: Percy makes a joking aggressive gesture toward Del, who reacts in fear, trips over Brutal's feet, and falls hard on the floor, hitting his head.
memories.memory_text: I saw Del jerk back in fear from Percy's gesture, trip over my feet, and fall hard on the floor, hitting his head, so I helped him up.

grounded_facts: Percy uses a falsely generous tone to tell Del to return to his cell, then follows it with a mocking aggressive gesture that frightens Del.
memories.memory_text: I heard Percy tell Del in a falsely generous tone to go back to his cell, and then I saw him bare his teeth and curl his fingers like he was going to grab Del, which scared him.

grounded_facts: After being assaulted by Billy, Percy is so terrified that he loses bladder control, visibly urinating in his pants.
memories.memory_text: I saw Percy get slammed against the bars by Billy, and he was so scared that he actually pissed himself right there.

grounded_facts: Billy grabs Percy, threatens him, strokes his hair, whispers sexually degrading remarks, kisses his ear, and gropes his crotch.
Billy grabs Percy, slams him against the cell bars, threatens him verbally, strokes his hair, kisses his ear, and gropes his crotch, causing extreme terror.
memories.memory_text: I saw Billy lunge out and grab Percy, slamming him against the cell bars with one arm around his throat while stroking his hair, whispering nasty things in his ear, then kissing it and groping his crotch—I could see the terror in Percy’s eyes and knew he thought he was going to die.

grounded_facts: Del laughs and loudly points out that Percy has urinated himself, drawing attention to his humiliation.
memories.memory_text: I heard Del laugh and point at Percy, shouting that he'd pissed his pants, making sure everyone saw how humiliated he was.

grounded_facts: Paul steps toward Percy and places a hand on his shoulder in an attempt to calm him.
memories.memory_text: I saw Paul step toward Percy and put a hand on his shoulder, trying to calm him down.

grounded_facts: Percy threatens to get the guards fired if they speak about the incident.
memories.memory_text: I heard Percy threaten us, saying he'd get us all fired if we talked about what happened.

grounded_facts: Paul declares that what happens on the Mile stays on the Mile, reinforcing the guards' collective decision not to report the incident.
memories.memory_text: I remember Paul declaring that what happens on the Mile stays on the Mile, and the rest of us nodding—we weren't going to talk.

grounded_facts: Percy deliberately stomps on Mr. Jingles, breaking the mouse's back, resulting in its apparent death.
Percy deliberately stomps on Mr. Jingles, killing the mouse in front of the guards and Del.
memories.memory_text: I saw Percy stomp on Mr. Jingles with his heel, and I heard the snap of the mouse's back breaking; then he just walked away while Del screamed in grief.

grounded_facts: Coffey responds to Del's emotional plea by miraculously healing Mr. Jingles.
Coffey uses supernatural means to revive Mr. Jingles, restoring the mouse to full health after its apparent death.
memories.memory_text: I saw Del pleading with Coffey to help Mr. Jingles after Percy stomped on him, and then I watched Coffey cup the mouse in his hands and somehow bring it back to life—I whispered 'Oh, dear Jesus. The tail. Look at the tail.' when I saw it move again.

grounded_facts: The day leading up to Delacroix's execution, marked by emotional farewells, the fate of Mr. Jingles, and escalating conflict with Percy.
memories.memory_text: I was there when Del was playing with Mr. Jingles, and I remember talking about what might happen to the mouse; later, after Percy killed it, I heard Paul say he was glad Mr. Jingles was okay, which felt wrong given what I'd seen.

grounded_facts: Paul and Brutal corner Percy in the execution chamber and force him to agree to transfer out in exchange for not exposing his prior misconduct.
Under duress, Percy agrees to transfer out of E Block after being threatened with exposure over his failure to act during Wild Bill's attack on Dean.
Paul confronts Percy in the execution chamber and threatens to expose his failure to act during Wild Bill's attack unless he agrees to transfer out.
memories.memory_text: I was there with Paul when we cornered Percy in the execution chamber, and I saw him agree to transfer out after Paul threatened to expose how he did nothing during Wild Bill's attack on Dean.

grounded_facts: Del asks Paul to take care of Mr. Jingles and ensure he is sent to Mouseville after the execution.
memories.memory_text: I was told to make sure Mr. Jingles would be sent to Mouseville after the execution, and Del made me promise to take care of him.

grounded_facts: Del hands over his pet mouse Mr. Jingles to Paul, who then transfers it to Coffey for safekeeping before the execution.
memories.memory_text: I saw Del hand over Mr. Jingles to Paul, and then Paul transferred the mouse to Coffey for safekeeping before the execution.

grounded_facts: Percy tells Del that Mouseville is a lie, destroying his hope in his final moments.
memories.memory_text: I heard Percy tell Del that Mouseville was a lie, just a fairy tale to keep him quiet, and I saw how it crushed him in his final moments.

grounded_facts: The formal execution of Eduard Delacroix in the electric chair, which goes horribly wrong due to sabotage.
memories.memory_text: I witnessed the execution of Eduard Delacroix in the electric chair, which went horribly wrong—there was screaming, fire, and he was still alive at one point.

grounded_facts: After realizing the sabotage, Paul forces Percy to watch the consequences of his actions.
memories.memory_text: I saw Paul grab Percy and force him to look, making him watch what he'd done.

grounded_facts: Due to the dry sponge, Delacroix is slowly burned alive during electrocution, screaming and convulsing until death.
memories.memory_text: I saw Delacroix screaming and convulsing in the chair, his face charring and the mask catching fire, and he didn't die quickly—I watched him suffer until his body finally went still.

grounded_facts: Brutal hands Percy the fire extinguisher and forces him to hose down the smoking corpse.
memories.memory_text: I took the fire extinguisher and shoved it into Percy's hands, telling him he was running the show and making him clean up the mess.

grounded_facts: Paul realizes the sponge was not soaked, understanding that Percy deliberately caused the botched execution.
memories.memory_text: I realized the sponge wasn't soaked and saw Percy turn away, so I forced him to face it and handed him the extinguisher, making him clean up what he did because I knew he had sabotaged the execution on purpose.

grounded_facts: Percy pretends to soak the sponge in brine but leaves it dry, causing a malfunction during electrocution.
memories.memory_text: I saw Percy pretend to soak the sponge but leave it dry, which caused the electrocution to malfunction.

grounded_facts: Percy admits he did not know the sponge was supposed to be wet, revealing his ignorance as the cause of the botched execution.
memories.memory_text: I heard Percy say he didn't know the sponge was supposed to be wet, which showed me he didn't understand a basic part of the procedure.

grounded_facts: Brutal physically assaults Percy in response to the botched execution, leading to a scuffle.
memories.memory_text: I hauled off and slugged Percy, and then a scuffle broke out when the others grabbed me to pull me off.

grounded_facts: Paul intervenes verbally to stop Brutal from further attacking Percy.
memories.memory_text: I was told to stop when Paul shouted 'Brutal, no!' as they were pulling me away from Percy.

grounded_facts: Paul makes a dark joke about Wharton singing, which breaks the tension and causes laughter.
memories.memory_text: I was there when Paul made that joke about Wharton singing—'Can he carry a tune, Hal?'—and it hit us all at once, the tension just broke and I laughed along with the others.

grounded_facts: Hal arrives and confronts the crew about the chaotic aftermath, demanding to know what happened.
memories.memory_text: I saw Hal come lunging down the stairs, furious, demanding to know what happened after the execution went wrong. He was shouting about the witnesses puking, the smell, and Wharton singing, and he kept asking us, 'What the hell happened?'

grounded_facts: Paul declares that Percy will submit a transfer request to Briar Ridge, effectively removing him from the team.
memories.memory_text: I saw Paul declare that Percy would submit a transfer request to Briar Ridge, making it clear he was being pushed out.

grounded_facts: Hal directly insults Percy and threatens his position, reinforcing his disapproval.
memories.memory_text: I witnessed Hal insult Percy directly, calling him a little asshole and demanding the transfer request be on his desk first thing.

grounded_facts: The immediate aftermath of Delacroix's botched execution, where the crew deals with emotional fallout and assigns blame.
memories.memory_text: I remember the chaos after Delacroix's botched execution—the tension, Hal coming down furious, the strange laughter that broke out, and me shoving Percy aside to wheel the body down the tunnel myself.

grounded_facts: Paul discloses that John Coffey healed him of a bladder infection, establishing Coffey's supernatural healing power as a credible phenomenon.
memories.memory_text: I heard Paul say that Coffey put his hands on him and took away his bladder infection, right there at the table.

grounded_facts: Paul appeals to Brutal's sense of justice and compassion to gain support for taking Coffey to Melinda.
memories.memory_text: Paul appealed to me, saying what's happening to Melinda is an offense to the eyes, ears, and heart, and I told him we don't know her like he and Jan do, but I could see he was asking a lot.

grounded_facts: Paul implies and the group begins to consider taking John Coffey to Melinda Moores for healing, despite the extreme risks.
memories.memory_text: I was there when Paul suggested taking John Coffey to Melinda Moores for healing, and though the idea seemed dangerous, we started talking about it seriously, weighing the risks of him escaping or us losing our jobs against the chance he could actually help her.

grounded_facts: Harry opposes the plan by emphasizing the danger of Coffey escaping and the moral burden of potential harm.
memories.memory_text: I heard Harry say we shouldn't forget Coffey is a murderer and asked what if he escapes, because he'd hate having a dead child on his conscience even more than losing his job or going to prison.

grounded_facts: A domestic meal shared by Paul, Jan, Brutal, Dean, and Harry, during which a serious moral and logistical discussion unfolds.
memories.memory_text: We were sharing a meal when the talk turned serious—Paul said he didn't think Coffey did it, and I remember worrying about the risks if we helped him, especially with what could happen if he escaped.

grounded_facts: Paul directly contradicts the accepted narrative of Coffey's guilt, introducing moral ambiguity.
Paul states he does not believe John Coffey murdered the children, challenging the foundational assumption of Coffey's imprisonment.
memories.memory_text: I heard Paul say he doesn't think Coffey did it at all, and he argued that God wouldn't give such a gift to a man who'd kill a child.

grounded_facts: Brutal takes morphine tablets from a locked cabinet in the infirmary dispensary and hides them in his pocket.
memories.memory_text: I took a few morphine tablets from the locked cabinet in the infirmary dispensary and slipped them into my pocket.

grounded_facts: Brutal gives five dollars to the nightshift orderly to ensure silence about his presence and actions.
memories.memory_text: I gave the nightshift orderly five dollars and told him I was never there, making sure he'd keep quiet about my actions.

grounded_facts: Brutal gives money to the orderly with the explicit request to be unremembered; the orderly accepts and affirms his complicity.
memories.memory_text: I slipped the orderly five bucks and told him I was never here, and he said for that amount, I was never nowhere.

grounded_facts: Paul crushes morphine pills into powder on a stainless steel gurney, and Brutus carefully transfers the powder onto a small sheet of paper.
memories.memory_text: I carefully scraped the morphine powder Paul had crushed from the gurney onto a small sheet of paper.

grounded_facts: Paul withholds the cola and demands Billy promise to behave before allowing him to drink.
memories.memory_text: I saw Paul hold the cola out of Billy's reach and demand a promise to behave before letting him drink it.

grounded_facts: Paul prepares a cola drink laced with morphine and gives it to Billy after securing his promise to behave, marking the beginning of the execution plan.
memories.memory_text: I was there when Paul prepared a cola with morphine and gave it to Billy after he promised to behave, which started the execution plan.

grounded_facts: Coffey quietly agrees to participate in the execution, shocking the guards.
Coffey quietly agrees to participate in the execution plan when asked indirectly.
memories.memory_text: I was there when Coffey quietly agreed to take part in the execution, saying he'd like to take a ride, and I saw the shock on the others' faces just like my own.

grounded_facts: Percy's possession of a 'Tijuana Bible' is revealed when his book falls, exposing the hidden pornographic material.
memories.memory_text: I saw Percy's book fall and caught a glimpse of that crude cartoon—Popeye and Olive Oyl in a filthy pose, the kind of thing they banned back in the day.

grounded_facts: Brutal ridicules Percy upon discovering the 'Tijuana Bible', undermining his dignity.
memories.memory_text: I mocked Percy right then, saying, 'Oooo, Poicy! What would your mother say?'—just to twist the knife after seeing what he was hiding.

grounded_facts: Brutal applies pain and threatens to mutilate Percy's ears to force compliance.
memories.memory_text: I twisted Percy's ears hard and told him I'd rip them off and use them for tea caddies if he didn't put his arms up.

grounded_facts: Percy is physically overpowered and forced into a canvas straitjacket by Paul, Brutal, and Harry.
memories.memory_text: I helped Paul and Harry overpower Percy and force him into a straitjacket after he tried to run.

grounded_facts: A punitive and humiliating intervention carried out by Paul, Brutal, and Harry to subdue Percy in Paul's office.
memories.memory_text: I was part of the push with Paul and Harry to bring Percy down—he tried to run, we wrestled him back and got the straitjacket on him fast.

grounded_facts: Percy, now restrained, begs Paul not to place him in the cell with Wild Bill.
After being restrained, Percy begs Paul not to place him in the cell with Wild Bill, revealing fear and vulnerability.
memories.memory_text: I saw Percy, all tied up and scared, beg Paul not to put him in the cell with Wild Bill—he was practically crying, showing how afraid he really was.

grounded_facts: After Percy's plea, Paul responds with a forceful shove, expressing anger and rejection.
memories.memory_text: I watched Paul respond by shoving Percy hard and angrily, making it clear he wasn't going to listen to his begging.

grounded_facts: Paul silences Percy by slapping tape over his mouth and shoving him into the restraint room.
memories.memory_text: I saw Paul slap tape over Percy's mouth and shove him into the restraint room.

grounded_facts: Brutal mocks Percy with a crude joke about Olive Oyl while locking him in the restraint room.
memories.memory_text: I mocked Percy with a crude joke about Olive Oyl while locking him in the restraint room, thrusting my hips and making the sound to taunt him.

grounded_facts: Percy is disarmed, gagged with tape, and locked in the restraint room by the guards as punishment for his actions toward Del.
memories.memory_text: I helped disarm Percy, saw him gagged with tape, and watched as we all slammed the door shut, locking him in the restraint room as punishment for what he did to Del.

grounded_facts: The guards unlock the gun safe, retrieve shotguns, and load them before proceeding down the Mile.
memories.memory_text: I helped unlock the gun safe, grabbed my shotgun, and loaded it before we headed down the Mile.

grounded_facts: Coffey is unlocked from his cell and brought out to be moved, as part of a covert prison operation.
memories.memory_text: I was there when they unlocked Coffey's cell and brought him out—we were moving him as part of the operation, and I helped get the team armed from the wall safe.

grounded_facts: A coordinated effort by the guards to secretly move Coffey while concealing their actions by framing noise on Percy and fabricating alibis.
memories.memory_text: We planned to move Coffey quietly by making noise seem like it was coming from the restraint room, and I was part of that effort with the others.

grounded_facts: Billy grabs Coffey's wrist and slurs a threatening question, initiating a disturbing physical and emotional reaction.
Billy suddenly grabs Coffey's wrist, triggering a strong, fearful reaction in Coffey as if experiencing a supernatural connection.
memories.memory_text: I saw Billy suddenly reach out and grab Coffey's wrist, and I watched how Coffey trembled like he was shocked, his eyes wide with horror as if something terrible passed between them.

grounded_facts: Coffey verbally identifies Billy as a 'bad man' twice, indicating deep moral revulsion and fear.
memories.memory_text: I heard Coffey say twice that Billy was a 'bad man,' his voice full of fear and disgust, like he'd seen something evil in him.

grounded_facts: Coffey is brought up from the tunnel beneath the prison wall and emerges into the night outside.
memories.memory_text: I saw Paul and the others bring Coffey up from the tunnel below, emerging into the night.

grounded_facts: A coordinated escape from the prison through a tunnel and side gate under cover of night.
memories.memory_text: I realized we were carrying out a coordinated escape through the tunnel and side gate under cover of night, though I didn't say it out loud.

grounded_facts: Coffey excitedly points out the constellation Cassie, shaped like a lady in a rocking chair, sharing his wonder with Paul.
memories.memory_text: I watched Coffey point at the stars in wonder and say to Paul, 'Look, boss! It's Cassie, the lady in the rocking chair!'

grounded_facts: Paul tells Coffey to be quiet to avoid detection during the escape.
memories.memory_text: I heard Paul tell Coffey to be quiet, saying, 'Shhh. John, you have to be quiet now,' to keep us from being detected.

grounded_facts: Brutal tells Coffey they see the lady in the stars to comfort him after Paul silences him.
memories.memory_text: After Paul quieted him, I told Coffey, 'We see her, John,' to comfort him and acknowledge the lady in the stars he was talking about.

grounded_facts: The group exits through a rarely used iron gate in the prison wall, beginning their escape across the fields.
memories.memory_text: I remember us slipping through the iron gate in the prison wall, moving fast across the fields under the cover of night as one of the dark figures in the group.

grounded_facts: Coffey misreads the guards' anxious looks and offers them leaves to smell, which they accept to appease him.
memories.memory_text: I noticed the guards giving Coffey anxious looks, and when he held out his hand for them to smell the leaves, I saw them comply just to keep him happy.

grounded_facts: A nighttime journey through the woods during which the guards escort Coffey to a hidden truck, uncover it, and prepare for vehicular travel.
The guards lead Coffey to a thicket where they remove branches to reveal a concealed old truck, preparing for the next stage of travel.
memories.memory_text: I was with the guards as we led Coffey through the woods at night to a thicket, where we removed branches and uncovered a battered old Farmall truck hidden in the brush, getting ready to switch from walking to driving.

grounded_facts: Coffey notices fireflies gathering around him playfully, interprets it as a sign of mutual affection, and shares this moment with the guards, who observe in awe and unease.
memories.memory_text: I saw Coffey laughing softly, his face lit up like a child's as he let a firefly weave in and out of his fingers, calling out to it gently, and I watched in uneasy awe as more gathered around him.

grounded_facts: Coffey explains to Paul that the fireflies are drawn to him because he loves them and they feel no hurtful thoughts, only happiness.
memories.memory_text: I heard Coffey tell Paul that the fireflies came to him because he loved them and they felt no hurtful thoughts—just happiness—and it struck me how sincerely he believed it.

grounded_facts: Harry gives Paul a look asking if they can leave, expressing discomfort with the surreal firefly scene.
memories.memory_text: I saw Harry give Paul a pleading look, asking without words if they could leave, clearly unsettled by the strange, glowing scene unfolding before us.

grounded_facts: Coffey climbs onto the back of the truck, followed by Paul and Brutal, marking the transition from walking to vehicular movement.
memories.memory_text: I climbed onto the back of the truck after Coffey, with Paul right behind me, and I could feel the shift from walking to getting ready to move out.

grounded_facts: When asked if he knows where they are going, Coffey responds that they are going to help a lady, showing unexplained awareness of their purpose.
memories.memory_text: I was on the truck when Paul asked Coffey if he knew where we were going, and Coffey said, 'Help a lady?'—which turned out to be right, even though he claimed he didn't know much of anything.

grounded_facts: Brutal expresses fear and urges Paul to turn back before approaching the house.
memories.memory_text: I felt scared and told Paul we could still turn back before we went up to the house.

grounded_facts: The group arrives at the Moore house in the truck, with headlights illuminating the isolated property at night.
memories.memory_text: I saw the headlights of our truck light up the Moore house as we arrived—it was isolated and dark, just us pulling in at night.

grounded_facts: An urgent nighttime visit by Paul, Brutal, and Coffey to the Moore household to provide help during a crisis.
memories.memory_text: I was there with Paul and Coffey when we made the urgent trip to the Moore house at night to help during a crisis.

grounded_facts: Hal confronts Paul and Brutal at gunpoint, demanding to know their intentions and suspecting a prison break.
memories.memory_text: I was with Paul when Hal suddenly appeared with a gun, demanding to know who was outside and if we were hostages—I could feel my heart pounding as he shouted at us.

grounded_facts: Melinda shouts from upstairs, cursing and demanding that the visitors be sent away, revealing her deteriorated mental state.
memories.memory_text: I heard Melinda shouting from upstairs, cursing and telling Hal to get rid of us, and it scared me how unhinged her voice sounded.

grounded_facts: Coffey gently instructs Melinda to remain still before initiating the healing.
memories.memory_text: I heard Coffey tell Melinda to be still and quiet before he started the healing.

grounded_facts: Paul tells Melinda that her X-ray was clear and there was no tumor.
memories.memory_text: I heard Paul tell Melinda that her X-ray was clear and there was no tumor.

grounded_facts: After healing Melinda, Coffey collapses into violent coughing fits, showing severe physical distress and requiring support from Brutal and Paul.
memories.memory_text: I saw Coffey collapse right after healing Melinda, coughing so hard he couldn't breathe, and I dropped down beside him, slapping his back and telling him to sick it up—whatever he'd taken from her, it was choking him. I could see he was retching, eyes watering, spit flying, and I knew he was in real trouble, so I helped him try to get back up.

grounded_facts: A supernatural healing event takes place at Melinda Moores' bedside, involving Coffey, her husband Hal, and Paul's group, resulting in her full recovery and Coffey's physical collapse.
memories.memory_text: I was there when Coffey healed Melinda at her bedside—Hal was present, and Paul's group was watching; after the healing, Coffey collapsed and I dropped to his side to help him.

grounded_facts: Coffey performs a supernatural act of healing, drawing illness from Melinda Moores through a kiss, restoring her to full health while visibly suffering the effects himself.
memories.memory_text: I saw Coffey kiss Melinda and draw the illness out of her, restoring her to full health, but he began coughing violently, dropped to his knees, and turned ashen gray, clearly suffering the effects himself.

grounded_facts: After being healed, Melinda regains full cognitive function, recalls recent events, and walks unaided to Coffey.
memories.memory_text: I saw Melinda regain her strength after the healing, push the covers aside, stand up, and walk unaided to Coffey, touching his face as he struggled.

grounded_facts: Melinda tells Coffey she dreamed of him, expressing a deep spiritual connection.
memories.memory_text: I heard Melinda tell Coffey that she dreamed of him, that they found each other in the dark.

grounded_facts: Melinda gives Coffey her necklace of St. Christopher as a token of gratitude and protection.
memories.memory_text: I saw Melinda give Coffey her St. Christopher necklace, telling him it would keep him safe, and then she hugged him tightly after putting it on him.

grounded_facts: Coffey is physically assisted from Moore's house to the truck's stakebed due to extreme physical weakness.
memories.memory_text: I helped Coffey out of Moore's house and up onto the truck's stakebed because he was so weak he could barely stand.

grounded_facts: Brutal privately tells Paul that Coffey will die soon, implying suicide, and that he won't be executed.
Brutal states that Coffey will die soon, likely by suicide, before reaching execution.
memories.memory_text: I told Paul that Coffey would never sit in Old Sparky, that he'd be dead on his bunk in a few days after swallowing that poison for a reason.

grounded_facts: Paul decides to take Coffey back to the prison block known as the Mile.
memories.memory_text: I heard Paul say, 'Let's get him back on the Mile,' so I knew he decided to take Coffey back to the prison block.

grounded_facts: A titled narrative segment marking Coffey's return to the prison block, symbolizing the final phase of his story.
memories.memory_text: I think we're bringing Coffey back to the Mile now, which might mean this is the final stretch of his story, though I'm not certain how it'll end.

grounded_facts: Paul slaps Percy and threatens him with physical harm and social exposure unless he remains silent about the events involving Del's execution.
memories.memory_text: I was there when Paul took the tape off Percy's mouth and slapped him hard, then threatened to have him beaten and even mutilated if he ever spoke about what happened with Del's execution, making it clear that no one would ever need to know but us.

grounded_facts: The guards confront Percy in the restraint room after leaving Coffey, threaten him into silence, and later witness his transformation and violent actions on the Mile.
memories.memory_text: I saw Percy get grabbed by Coffey through the bars, then watched as strange black things flowed into him, lights exploded, and he became vacant—later, I helped tackle him when he went after Wild Bill with a gun, and I saw the black bugs leave his body and vanish into the air.

grounded_facts: Coffey pleads with Paul to take his hand and forcibly shares a vision of Wild Bill's crime, revealing the truth about the twins' murder.
memories.memory_text: I remember that Coffey pleads with Paul to take his hand and forcibly shares a vision of Wild Bill's crime, revealing the truth about the twins' murder.

grounded_facts: Coffey forcibly transfers the black 'insects' (evil essence) from himself into Percy, healing himself but driving Percy into a catatonic state, then reveals Wild Bill's guilt by sharing a vision of the crime with Paul.
After being released from the straitjacket and regaining his belongings, Percy is seized by Coffey, undergoes a supernatural transfer, and then mindlessly shoots Wild Bill six times in the chest.
memories.memory_text: I saw Coffey grab Percy through the bars and force those black insects from his own body into Percy's mouth and nose, healing himself while Percy went blank and lifeless; then I watched Percy walk up the Mile like a ghost and shoot Wild Bill six times, and later, I learned from Paul how Coffey had seen Wild Bill's guilt in a vision and shared it with him.

grounded_facts: Coffey compels Paul to hold his hand, forcing him to witness a detailed vision of Wild Bill murdering the Detterick twins, confirming Coffey's innocence and the true nature of the crime.
memories.memory_text: I infer that Coffey compels Paul to hold his hand, forcing him to witness a detailed vision of Wild Bill murdering the Detterick twins, confirming Coffey's innocence and the true nature of the crime.

grounded_facts: Paul discloses having read the file and confirms that Wild Bill Wharton was hired at the Detterick farm in the spring to repair the barn, establishing his connection to the victims' family.
memories.memory_text: I remember Paul telling me he read the file and confirmed that Wharton was hired by the Detterick father last spring to help repair the barn, just cheap labor like any drifter.

grounded_facts: Paul informs the group that Wharton worked at the Detterick farm, establishing a factual link between Wharton and the victims.
memories.memory_text: I heard Paul inform the group that Wharton had been at the Detterick farm before the murders, and that he came back a month later and took the girls, which established his direct connection to the crime.

grounded_facts: Jan suggests fabricating a confession by Wharton to stop Coffey's execution, with Brutal backing it up to explain Percy's actions.

grounded_facts: Jan shifts from legal solutions to demanding direct action, urging the guards to help Coffey escape permanently.

grounded_facts: A group conversation at Paul's house at dusk where Jan, Paul, and the guards debate Wharton's role in the Detterick girls' murders and possible actions to save Coffey.

grounded_facts: The guards collectively reject Jan's escape proposal, citing Coffey's size, recognizability, and the inevitable consequences for their careers and families.
memories.memory_text: I witnessed the guards reject Jan's proposal, saying Coffey was too recognizable and that helping him escape would ruin our lives.

grounded_facts: Frustrated and heartbroken, Jan denounces the guards as murderers and cowards for refusing to act to save Coffey.
Jan directly accuses Paul of becoming a murderer if he proceeds with Coffey's execution, equating him morally with Wharton.
memories.memory_text: I heard Jan scream at us, calling the guards murderers and cowards for not stopping Coffey's execution, and she looked right at Paul when she said he'd be no better than Wharton if he went through with it.

grounded_facts: Coffey expresses his desire for a specific last meal before execution, indicating acceptance of his fate.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Coffey that he'd like meatloaf, mashed potatoes with gravy, and maybe some okra for his last meal, and I remember him saying he wasn't picky.

grounded_facts: Coffey refuses the offer of a preacher but invites Paul to pray with him, signaling trust and emotional intimacy.
memories.memory_text: I heard Paul ask Coffey if he wanted a preacher, and Coffey said no—but then he told Paul he’d kneel and pray with him, and I remember Paul sounding surprised when Coffey said that.

grounded_facts: Paul questions the morality of the execution and suggests letting Coffey escape, testing his own conscience.
memories.memory_text: I asked John what he really wanted, if he wanted me to take him out of here and let him run away, just to see how far he could get.

grounded_facts: Coffey comforts Paul by framing the execution as an act of kindness, alleviating Paul's moral burden.
memories.memory_text: I remember John taking my hand and telling me to tell God it was a kindness I done, saying he could feel how much I was hurting and worrying, but that I should let it go because he wanted it over.

grounded_facts: Coffey reveals his deep emotional and psychic exhaustion, affirming his wish for execution as a release.
memories.memory_text: I heard John say he was tired—tired of being on the road, lonely, and worn down by all the pain in the world, like pieces of glass in his head—and I knew he truly wanted the execution to be his release.

grounded_facts: Paul and the guards visit Coffey to discuss final arrangements before his execution.
memories.memory_text: I unlocked Coffey's cell and went in with Paul to talk about his final arrangements, and I asked him if there was anything he wanted because there must be something we could do for him before the end.

grounded_facts: Coffey shares that he has never seen a motion picture, leading to a poignant moment of human longing.
memories.memory_text: I remember Coffey telling me he'd never seen a flicker show, and it struck me how much he'd missed.

grounded_facts: Coffey reassures the guards that he will be all right, attempting to ease their emotional burden.
memories.memory_text: I heard Coffey tell us he'd be all right, trying to comfort me and the others as we walked him down.

grounded_facts: Paul temporarily takes custody of Coffey's religious medal before the execution.
memories.memory_text: I took custody of Coffey's St. Christopher medal just before the execution, telling him I'd return it afterward.

grounded_facts: Coffey recounts a dream in which Mr. Jingles brings joy to children, including the murdered Detterick girls, in a peaceful afterlife setting.
memories.memory_text: I heard Coffey describe a dream where Mr. Jingles brought joy to children, including the Detterick girls, in a peaceful place where they were laughing and unharmed.

grounded_facts: Coffey, Paul, Dean, Brutal, and Harry kneel together in prayer before the execution.
memories.memory_text: I hesitated when Dean knelt, but then I joined him, Harry, Paul, and Coffey in prayer before the execution.

grounded_facts: Brutal urges Coffey to feel the love from those who don't hate him, offering emotional support.
memories.memory_text: I told Coffey to feel how we feel, that we don't hate him, hoping he could sense the love instead of the hatred around him.

grounded_facts: Marjorie verbally attacks Coffey, wishing him prolonged suffering.
memories.memory_text: I heard Marjorie scream at Coffey, telling him to die slow and calling him a raping baby-killer, wishing him to suffer twice over.

grounded_facts: Coffey pleads not to have the mask placed over his face, revealing his fear of the dark.
memories.memory_text: I saw Coffey beg not to have the mask put over his face, pleading that he was afraid of the dark, and it struck me how vulnerable he was in that moment.

grounded_facts: Paul hears Coffey's final mental message about love being used as a weapon in the world.

memories.memory_text: I saw how Coffey struggled and spoke about the hate he felt, and how he feared the dark—showing he knew what was coming and was trying to face it.

memories.memory_text: I remember being called John Coffey, like the drink, only not spelt the same. I don't know if they remember me, but I was there, and it was a hard time.
I was holding the little girls, tryin' to make 'em wake up, but they was cold and didn't move no more. I kept howlin' 'cause it hurt so bad inside, like my heart was tearin' apart.
I felt it deep in my chest, somethin' awful comin'—I had to warn them, kept sayin' 'Careful, careful,' pressin' my face to the bars, but Boss Paul just looked back puzzled-like.
I don't know how I knew, but I felt Boss Paul's pain inside me too, like a fire in my hands, and I just reached out soft-like, whisperin' I needed to help.

I smelled that cornbread coming, sweet and warm, and when Paul brought it close, I saw the tears in my eyes had fallen on the blanket. He said it was from his missus, on account of helping him with the hurt down there, and I asked if she was pleased—she was, several times.

I gave a piece to Del and Mr. Jingles 'cause Paul said it was mine to share, but when Billy hollered for some, I looked at Paul and then kept the rest—digging in with my fingers, smiling like I wasn't scared, even though his words stung like bees.
Poor Del. Poor old Del. I could feel it from here, all that hurt and fire inside him, even though I was on the Mile. It made me so tired, boss, dog tired.
They was talking 'bout a sick lady, Melinda Moores... I heard my name in the quiet, like they wonderin' if I could help her with my hands.
They were afraid to help Melinda, worried about their jobs and what might happen if I went with them.
I felt it when they gave him the drink, like a shadow moving through the dark. I said I'd like to take a ride, 'cause I know what's coming, and it can't be stopped.
I asked the boss if we was goan for the ride now, hopin' it meant somethin' good, somethin' true.
When that man grabbed my arm, I felt it deep inside—darkness, hate, all twisted up. I had to say it: you're a bad man. Then I said it again, 'cause it wouldn't leave my heart.
I saw that chair, all dark and still, and I felt the pieces of them still stuck inside it—I could hear them screaming, even though nobody else did.
Say. This is fun. I reached out and touched the walls as we went along, feeling the cold stone under my fingers while the lights passed over me.
I looked up and seen Cassie, the lady in the rocking chair, up in the sky—her face was made of stars, and I felt my breath catch inside me.
I seen little lights moving in the fields—fireflies, dancing like they was happy—and I didn't know such pretty things still lived out here.
I held out my hand and let the little fireflies dance through my fingers, blinking like happy stars. I asked them where Mrs. Firefly was, and they came right to me, like they knew I loved them.
When Boss Paul asked if I knew where we was going, I said I was helping a lady. I don't know how I knew it—truth is, I don't understand much at all—but it felt right to say.
I stepped into the headlights and said, 'Just to help, boss, that's all,' then took the gun from Hal's hands and gave it to Paul.
I walked past the warden into the house, even though Harry was pulling on my arm, and I could hear the woman crying upstairs after the glass broke, and I knew we had to go in.
I told Hal to be quiet, 'cause I had to go up them stairs, had to get to that voice, even if my legs was shaking and I didn't want to scare her.
I bent down to her, soft-like, and whispered for her to be still, then kissed her on the forehead and moved to her lips—felt the sickness pull out of her and into me, like smoke through a straw.
After the kiss, I felt it—something thick and dark filling my chest, making it hard to breathe, like I was choking on fire and shadows, and I started to shake from the weight of what I took.
I couldn't hardly stand, boss. My legs was shaking like leaves, and the fellas had to hold me up all the way to the truck.
I heard Brutal say I wouldn't last a few days, boss. I didn't move, but I heard him plain—said I'd be dead on my bunk.
I felt the bad inside me, like a sickness from Wild Billy, and I couldn't stand it no more. I had to pass it on, had to make it stop.
After I kissed him, I felt stronger, like the light coming back. I saw Percy shaking, his eyes gone empty, and I knew the dark had taken him instead.
I heard Boss Paul talk about Wild Bill taking the girls, and how they couldn't make it right for me. It made my heart hurt, like bees stinging inside my chest.
Paul was told to talk to me, to find out what I wanted.
I told Boss Paul I was tired—tired of the road, tired of the pain in the world, like glass in my head. I held his hand and said it was a kindness, what he had to do.
I thought hard and then said it—I ain't never seen me a flicker show. Later, I remember the light on my face, moving pictures dancing on my skin, like magic.
Why, they's angels. Angels. Just like up in heaven... I seen Fred and Ginger dancin’ on that screen, movin’ so smooth and bright, like light itself was lovin’ them.
I told Boss Paul I was sorry for what I am, and Miss Marjorie called me a monster, screaming she hoped it hurt like hell.
I asked Boss Paul not to let them put the mask over my face because I's afraid of the dark, and he told Brutal to stop.
I had to give a little of myself to Paul, so he could see what Wild Bill done. I felt it pass, like a breath leaving, but warm.

memories.memory_text: I looked out at the rain and felt the weight of sixty years pressing down, wondering if I could finally speak the words I’d carried alone for so long—then I told Elaine I was in charge of death row, and that we called it the Green Mile.

I felt the weight of it when the current hit—Bitterbuck’s body jerking against the straps, the air thick with the smell of brine and something burning, and all I could hear was his breath turning into silence.
I locked eyes with Brutal as we stood there—no words, just that grim understanding passing between us, both of us holding the same unbearable weight.

I walked into Hal's office and saw him staring out the window, struggling to speak about the new prisoner—Wharton—before breaking down and telling me about the tumor in Melinda's brain, the size of a lemon, inoperable, and how she'd be gone by Christmas. I just stood there, helpless, watching one of the strongest men I knew come completely apart.

I was rushing to the outhouse, couldn't hold it, so I stopped by the woodpile to relieve myself—and then the pain hit, the worst I've ever felt, like my body was tearing itself apart; I dropped to my knees, barely caught myself, and pressed my hand over my mouth to keep from screaming.
I rushed in to help when Billy attacked Dean, but he spun and kicked me hard in the groin—my bladder pain exploded like it had a mind of its own, and I collapsed, unable to move.
Even through the pain, I heard Coffey whispering 'Careful' from his cell—his voice kept rising, urgent, like he knew something terrible was about to happen, and he was trying to warn me.
I didn't go to the doctor yesterday—I just told Jan that to her face, and the look she gave me said everything.

I sat on Burt Hammersmith’s back porch, sipping a cold root beer Cynthia brought me, and asked if John Coffey had ever done anything like that before—trying to sound casual, though my gut twisted with doubt.
Del looked me in the eye and asked me to take care of Mr. Jingles, and I nodded—just a quiet promise, but it weighed on me like a vow I’d have to carry long after he was gone.
Del handed Mr. Jingles to me so gently, and when the mouse stepped onto my shoulder without fear, I remember thinking how small and trusting life could be—even here, even now.
I lay there in the dark, unable to sleep, and told Jan I love her—how I don't know what I'd do if she were gone.
After telling her I love her, I said I wanted to have the boys over tomorrow—something in me shifted, like I needed to act, to bring us together again.

I pulled the straitjacket from behind my back and told Percy it was payback—then Brutal and Harry helped me grab him when he tried to run. We wrestled him down, and when he finally raised his arms, we got the canvas on him fast.

After we had him strapped, Percy turned to me with tears in his eyes and begged, 'Please, Paul. Don't put me in with Wild Bill.' I just looked at him and said, 'You would think that,' before shoving him hard.

I stepped forward with the tape in my hand and told Percy we could and we were going to do this—he couldn't stop us. I slapped the tape over his mouth and shoved him into the restraint room, his muffled sounds fading as we shut the door.

Billy's arm shot out and grabbed Coffey's wrist—I saw Coffey flinch like he'd been shocked, his eyes wide with horror. I pulled Billy's hand off, and when the contact broke, Coffey flinched again, still trembling as he whispered, 'He's a bad man.'

When we brought Coffey into the chamber, he froze at the sight of Old Sparky and whispered that the dead were still in there, screaming—I felt the weight of that chair like I never had before, and for the first time, it truly haunted me.

I had to quiet John when he whispered and pointed at the stars—called them Cassie, the lady in the rocking chair. Out there in the dark, with the fireflies and the guards on the tower, I couldn't let him draw attention, not with the escape underway.

I remember how heavy John felt as we dragged him to the truck, his legs barely holding him—like a man already halfway gone. When Brutal said he’d be dead on his bunk in a few days, I knew it wasn’t fear or weakness; if he chose to die, he’d earned that right.

I ripped the tape off Percy's mouth, fast and hard—he flinched, eyes watering, and I didn't care. When he started screaming, I slapped him down and pulled him up by the collar, making sure he knew I was in control.

After we got Coffey settled and the others started smiling, I thought we’d pulled it off—then Dean burst in, panicked, saying Wild Bill was waking up, and I felt that fragile relief shatter in an instant.

I read the file and it made sense—Wharton had been causing trouble for years, even since he was ten, with vandalism and fires. Their father had hired him to repair the barn the spring before, just cheap labor, another drifter passing through.

Jan looked at me and said I could stop the execution, get Coffey a new trial, but I had to ask her—on what? A vision? I felt the weight of it, knowing the truth but having no proof that would hold up.

I sat at the kitchen table late at night, beer in hand, the radio playing softly, and told Jan I was afraid I'd damned myself by executing John Coffey—she touched my face and said my name like it broke her heart.

I sat with Coffey in his cell, heart pounding, and asked him if he wanted me to help him escape—really asked him—because I couldn't bear the thought of taking a miracle to the electric chair just because it was my job.
I reached for John's St. Christopher medal, feeling the weight of it in my hand before slipping it into my pocket—he let me take it without protest, trusting me even then.
John told me he dreamed about Del's mouse going to Mouseville, with kids laughing at his tricks. He laughed, then grew more serious as he spoke.
I drove home in the dark, hands on the wheel, but I couldn't feel anything—my chest was hollow, like my heart had stopped working long before I reached the house.
I sat in the car for a moment, not ready to move, then walked to the house and let Jan hold me—she didn’t say anything, but I finally broke down and just cried against her.

That was the last execution I ever took part in. I couldn't do it anymore after John Coffey. Brutal felt the same—we both left and took jobs with Boys' Correctional. Catch 'em young, that became my motto.

Elaine pointed out the math doesn't work—how could I have had a grown son in 1935 if I'm still alive now? I saw she was starting to question everything, and I knew then it was time. I asked if she felt up to a walk.
I got down on the floor and called to him—'Come over here, boy'—and held out the spool. Mr. Jingles looked at it, then started moving toward it, slow and stiff, but he kept going.

I didn't say a word about how long he's lived or why—I just watched him struggle to bring the spool back, breathing hard, and knew Elaine was seeing what I've carried all these years: the impossible truth of time not taking its toll the way it should.
I placed a rose on Elaine's casket, feeling the weight of her gone like all the rest, and I knew again—it's my punishment for letting John Coffey die, for killing a miracle of God.

dialogue_exemplars: I'll die eventually, I imagine. I have no illusions of immortality. But I will have wished for death long before death finds me.

They usually call death row the Last Mile, but we called ours the Green Mile, because the floor was the color of faded limes. We had the electric chair then. Old Sparky, we called it. (beat) I've lived a lot of years, Ellie, but 1935 takes the prize. That was the year I had the worst urinary infection of my life. That was also the year of John Coffey, and the two dead girls...
On the day of my judgement, when I stand before God, and He asks me why did I kill one of his true miracles, what am I gonna say? That is was my job? My job?

We know people, too, are you so foolish you don't realize that? People with friends and loved ones doing time in this prison. People who'd be happy to amputate you nose or your penis just so someone they care about could get an extra three hours in the exercise yard every week.

I think about all the people I've loved, now long gone. I think about my beautiful Jan, and how I lost her so many years ago. I think about all of us walking our own Green Mile, each in our own time. But one thought, more than any other, keeps me awake most nights... (beat) ...if he could make a mouse live so long, how much longer do I have?
That's as good a word as any. He infected us both, didn't he, Mr. Jingles. With life. (beat) I'm a hundred and five years old, Elaine. I was forty the year John Coffey walked the Green Mile.
What's with you? Seeing a man die isn't enough? You gotta be close enough to smell his nuts cook?
Go ahead. I promise you'll leave your share of blood on the floor.
You're about ten seconds away from spending the rest of your life in the padded room.
--and how you pissed yourself like a frightened little girl. Yes, we'll talk, that's a given--but, Percy, mind me now...we'll also see you beaten within an inch of your life.

God, please help us finish what we've started, and please welcome this man, John Coffey--like the drink, but not spelled the same--into heaven and give him peace. Please help us to see him off the best we can and let nothing go wrong. Amen.
...that's my punishment, you see? My punishment for letting John Coffey ride the lightning...for killing a miracle of God...
Little Percy called his aunt and squealed like a schoolroom sissy. He also mention he assaulted a prisoner this morning out of sheer petulance? Broke three fingers on Eduard Delacroix's left hand.
What's happening to her is an offense, Brutal. To the eyes and the ears and the heart.

No. But a man who does a thing like that has often developed a taste for it over time. Occurred to me it might be easy enough to follow his backtrail and find out. A man his size, and colored to boot, can't be that hard to trace.

relations.relation_summary: Paul and John Coffey share a deeply empathetic and spiritually charged relationship defined by mutual trust, compassion, and transformative acts of care. These actions reflect Paul’s recognition of Coffey’s humanity and emotional needs, transcending their institutional roles as guard and prisoner. Coffey, in turn, shows profound trust in Paul—seeking his permission, requesting physical contact, and initiating prayer together. The emotional dynamic is reciprocal: Paul expresses concern for Coffey’s distress and ultimately prays for his peaceful passage into heaven, while Coffey heals Paul’s illness and comforts him emotionally during the execution. Key events solidify this bond, including Coffey’s supernatural healing of Paul, their shared prayer, and the moment their hands clasp during the execution sequence—acts that carry spiritual and emotional weight. The relationship evolves from a guarded institutional dynamic into one of deep mutual respect and spiritual kinship. Coffey’s final moments are shared almost exclusively with Paul, underscoring their unique connection. The evidence confirms a relationship rooted in empathy, spiritual exchange, and moral solidarity, where both characters influence each other’s emotional and spiritual states in profound ways.

As coworkers within the prison system, Del addresses Paul as 'boss,' and Paul asserts control by instructing Del to mind his own business, establishing a clear superior-subordinate dynamic. This power structure is complicated by recurring evidence of empathy and protection: Paul expresses concern for Del's fate regarding his execution, refuses to shut down the process while Del is still alive, and offers physical reassurance through a squeeze on Del's arm. These actions suggest Paul feels a moral or emotional responsibility toward Del, transcending their professional roles. Despite this, tension exists—Del admonishes Paul and challenges his authority, indicating conflict over boundaries and decision-making. Their shared events reflect both care and strain: Paul delivers Del's share, tells him to rest, and informs him about an upcoming audience for Mr. Jingles, an act that sparks pride and preparation in Del, highlighting how Paul's communication directly influences Del's emotional state and behavior. Del’s request that Paul take the mouse to Florida further demonstrates trust in Paul beyond duty, implying a bond of collaboration and personal reliance. While conflict surfaces around authority, the cumulative evidence shows a relationship evolving from a strictly professional hierarchy toward one imbued with mutual emotional investment, where Paul increasingly acts as a protector and Del responds with trust and emotional openness. The relationship thus balances institutional power dynamics with genuine human empathy, shaping both characters’ actions in ethically charged situations.

Paul and Mr. Jingles share a deeply affectionate and nurturing relationship, characterized by consistent care and emotional attachment. Key events reinforce this dynamic: Paul actively searches for and retrieves Mr. Jingles, carrying him back up the Green Mile, demonstrating protective behavior. The evidence confirms an enduring, emotionally resonant connection rooted in mutual trust and care.

The relationship between Paul and Billy is defined by intense hostility and mutual confrontation, marked by physical and verbal aggression. Social relationship evidence shows Paul confronting and threatening Billy, including drawing a revolver and warning of padded room confinement, asserting authority in a coercive manner. Billy responds with violent resistance, exemplified by his powerful kick to Paul's groin, indicating deep defiance and rejection of Paul's control. Their shared events reinforce this adversarial dynamic: Paul repeatedly performs actions of physical restraint—dragging Billy from his cell, applying a straitjacket, and grabbing him by the feet—while Billy undergoes these acts with resistance. Despite this, they engage in a direct dialogue about Wild Bill Hickock, suggesting a brief moment of non-confrontational interaction, though Billy's defensive tone implies continued tension. There is no evidence of reconciliation or positive evolution; instead, the relationship remains entrenched in a power struggle, with Paul attempting to enforce discipline and Billy resisting through aggression. The emotional dynamic is one of mutual distrust and antagonism, influencing Paul’s decisions to escalate control measures and Billy’s to retaliate physically. The evidence is insufficient to confirm any underlying respect, hidden alliance, or transformative arc in their relationship.

memories.memory_text: I rapped Coffey with my baton to make him move faster into the cell—just a sharp tap, but he flinched like a whipped dog. Felt good, showing him and Paul I’m not scared to handle him.
Paul told me to shut up like I was some grunt, not staff—like I didn’t matter. I kept slapping the baton in my hand, letting him feel it; he can’t push me around, not with my connections.
I let out a roar and hurled my baton like a spear at that damn mouse—it shot past so close it ruffled its fur, but the little bastard ducked. Everyone jumped, startled, and the thing bolted.
I stomped after it, leaping and missing with every step, hearing the cons yell from their cells—then it slipped under the door. I slammed my fist and fumbled with my keys, furious it got away.
I laid the last trap down with the bacon, crept back to the desk, and held my breath—every scrap and trap leading right to where I knew that thing would come out. I was ready this time.

I saw it looking at me from under the desk—then it just sat there, like it was laughing. When I charged, it zipped past me again, and after I missed, Coffey said something... I couldn't even think, just started kicking the door.
I asked what I was supposed to do during the rehearsal, and Paul just told me to watch and learn like I was some damn trainee.
I saw them putting something on the headpiece and couldn't help asking about the sponge—nobody explained it, but I could see it mattered.
I pressed close to the mesh, eyes straining to see through the partition as the current hit—he jerked hard against the straps, and I wanted to be closer, needed to see every second of it.
I gave the dead Indian a little squeeze on the cheek, just to see what would happen—then Brutal came in like a bull and knocked my hand away, shoved me aside like I was nothing.
I told Paul straight—I want Brutal's spot for the next execution, and if he says no, I might just stick around for good. I saw the look on his face, like I'd grown a second head.
I wasn't there when Hal broke down about his wife's tumor—I only heard bits later, and it made me uneasy, like the whole place was cracking open.
I was trying to piss by the woodpile and this pain—this unbearable pain—hit me like a sledgehammer, dropped me to my knees, and I had to bite my hand to keep from screaming.
I mocked that spaced-out killer, jittering like he was in the chair—Bzzzzzzzzt-zap!—and told him he'd die with his knees bent, just to see him flinch.
I stood in the doorway and couldn't move when Billy came through, screaming and choking Dean—I just froze, staring, until Harry shoved me aside.
I saw Del strutting past like he'd won the damn lottery, all puffed up about his mouse trick—rolled my eyes and smirked because this whole thing was just another circus.

I flipped the switch for the mock execution and heard Van Hay say 'That's that,' then waited—Paul finally gave me the nod, said I did good, real professional, and the others came over slapping my back like I'd earned it.
I told Del to pop back in his cell, and for a second I meant it kindly—actually felt like part of the block, like I belonged. The look on his face… he didn’t know what to do with it.

Wild Bill grabbed me, slammed me against the bars—I couldn’t breathe, I squealed, thought I was dead. Then he touched me, kissed my ear, and squeezed… I ran, cringing, and I could feel the wetness down my leg.
I brought my heel down hard on the little bastard—felt the snap under my boot. He stopped moving right away, just a twitch.
I looked at Brutal and Paul, smiled—told them I knew I'd get him sooner or later. Then I walked off, not even looking back.
I said 'Roll on two' before Paul could stop it, watching the current hit Del—his body jerked forward hard, too hard, and the sound wasn't right, not steady like it should be.
I saw the smoke first—curling up from under the cap, then through the mask, and I knew the sponge was dry, but I didn't say a word.
I was trying to explain—the sponge, the procedure, I didn’t know—then Brutal just lunged and hit me, my lip split against my teeth, and I stumbled back before the others grabbed him.

Hal stared at my bloody lip, then asked me if I had anything to say—like he already knew I was the one to blame—and when I repeated I didn’t know, he mocked me and told me to have a transfer request on his desk by morning.
I kicked back in Paul's chair with my boots up, flipping through some dumb book about mental patients—just to show I could.

I was reading in Paul's office when they came in and cornered me—Paul had that straitjacket behind his back like they'd planned it. I tried to run, but Harry grabbed me and spun me around, and then they were all over me.

The book fell open and that damn Tijuana Bible spilled out—Olive Oyl and Popeye—right in front of them. I begged Paul, voice breaking, not to put me in with Wild Bill, but he just shoved me like he didn't care at all.

I remember the tape slapped over my mouth, the burn of it on my skin, and being shoved backward into the dark room while they laughed—my breath loud in my nose, muffled screams they didn’t care about.
They had me taped up and on the floor, and when Paul ripped the tape off my mouth, I couldn't stop the tears from coming—I just wanted out of that straitjacket, now.

After Paul slapped me and yanked me back up, I heard him threaten to have my nose or penis cut off—something about prisoners doing favors for guards’ families—and I couldn’t even process it, like the words were crawling through my skull.
I can't move, I can't speak—lights flashing in my face, voices yelling, but it's like I'm buried under concrete and can't get out.
I remember being dragged in by the orderlies, my feet barely moving, then left alone at the window—just like that, no warning, no choice.
I'm staring out the window, and the gate says 'Briar Ridge Mental Hospital'—this is it, my last stop, though I keep telling myself I won't stay long.
